Baby & Child

When school performance drops: finding the right support

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A lower mark, unfinished work or growing reluctance to attend school can mean different things. Start by finding out what has changed and which tasks have become difficult. The aim is to understand the obstacles and help your child learn, rather than turn a report card into a verdict on their intelligence, character or future.

Describe the change before deciding on a cause

Compare the current difficulty with your child’s usual pattern. Is it new, or has reading, writing or mathematics been hard for a long time? Does it affect one subject or most lessons? Ask the teacher for examples of classwork, attendance and the help already tried. A single disappointing test and a continuing loss of progress need different conversations.

Look beyond the final grade. A child might understand an idea aloud but struggle to write it down, miss instructions, leave work unfinished or be absent when a skill is taught. Record a few examples and include tasks that go well. This gives an assessment something useful to investigate without starting from an assumed diagnosis.

Hear the child’s account without making school a test of worth

Choose a calm moment and ask which part of the day feels difficult, confusing or worrying. Allow time to answer, and offer another trusted adult if talking to you is hard. Avoid labels such as lazy or unintelligent, threats and comparisons with siblings. Describe your concern about their experience rather than demanding an immediate explanation for every mark.

Keep strengths and interests visible. Notice a useful strategy, a question asked or an effort to return to a difficult task. For an older child, discuss subject and training choices together, including practical requirements and their interests. Their education should not be a way of fulfilling an adult’s unrealised ambitions, and a particular qualification cannot guarantee a satisfying life.

Check health, hearing, vision and missed learning

Arrange a review with the child’s usual healthcare professional for persistent or marked difficulties, especially alongside symptoms or a change in health. Mention headaches, trouble seeing the board, difficulty hearing instructions, fatigue, pain or frequent absence. Bring a medicine list and relevant developmental or exposure history. Do not stop a prescription because you suspect it affects concentration.

Conditions such as asthma, anaemia, thyroid disease or seizures may affect learning directly, through symptoms, treatment or time away from class. This is a reason for individual assessment, not a request for every possible blood test. A past prenatal exposure does not establish the explanation for today’s grades. Ask what examination, sensory check or referral fits the actual findings.

Separate learning needs from a judgment about ability

Persistent difficulty with decoding words, understanding language, spelling, writing or number skills may need an educational assessment. A learning disability does not mean low intelligence. Speech and language needs can affect following explanations as well as speaking. Ask which skill is difficult and what specialist teaching or speech-language input could address it.

ADHD, autism and other developmental conditions may be relevant for some children, but a drop in grades diagnoses none of them and does not show what a child can ultimately learn. If attention or behaviour is a concern, share examples across settings. Keep the question broad enough to consider coexisting needs rather than assuming one label explains everything.

Consider language and access to teaching

A child learning the language used at school may need language support alongside subject teaching. Using more than one language does not itself cause a communication disorder. Tell the assessment team which languages the child uses, with whom and for how long. Skills in a less familiar classroom language should not be treated as a complete measure of ability.

Ask how an evaluation will account for language, cultural experience, interrupted schooling and opportunities to learn. Appropriate interpreting or language-informed assessment may be needed. Also identify practical barriers, such as unavailable materials or difficulty reaching school. These call for support and a workable access plan, rather than a conclusion that the family does not value education.

Ask about stress and safety at home and school

Bereavement, conflict, family changes or financial strain can make learning harder. Their presence does not prove a single cause, and separation does not mean a child must do badly. Persistent worry, low mood, withdrawal or a loss of enjoyment deserve attention in their own right. Share relevant changes with a clinician and a trusted school contact without making the child responsible for adult problems.

Ask privately about feeling frightened of an adult, humiliation, bullying or exclusion by peers. Falling grades and avoiding school can be warning signs, but they are not specific to bullying, and some children show no obvious signs. Take a report of mistreatment seriously and arrange a safe school contact and follow-up. Suspected abuse or violence needs prompt local safeguarding help; immediate danger needs emergency help.

Review sleep and devices in the context of the whole day

Notice bedtime, waking, daytime sleepiness and whether schoolwork is regularly pushing sleep aside. Insufficient sleep can affect attention and learning. Aim for a consistent opportunity to sleep and tell the clinician about ongoing sleep problems. More time at a desk is not automatically helpful if the child is exhausted.

Ask what digital use is doing for the child and what it may be displacing. Devices can provide learning tools and social connection as well as distractions. Agree on ways to reduce interruptions during work and protect sleep, while keeping necessary educational access. A phone is not automatically the cause of a decline, and removing it cannot guarantee recovery.

Start small changes while arranging assessment

Agree on an achievable homework time and the least distracting space available. Check that instructions and materials are accessible, allow sensible breaks and tell the teacher if work repeatedly takes much longer than expected. Ask for help with the particular subject or task instead of adding more of the same work as punishment. A quiet room alone will not resolve every learning difficulty.

The school and healthcare team have different, complementary roles. Educational evaluation may examine academic skills and progress with teaching; a clinician reviews health and development and selects further referrals. A psychologist, learning specialist or speech-language professional may contribute when relevant. Ask what help can begin while waiting, and which local process applies rather than assuming one named plan is available everywhere.

Agree how you will know whether help is working

Choose a concrete aim with the child and school, such as understanding a particular reading task or attending a lesson more comfortably. Record what support is being provided and arrange a review date and contact person. Include the child’s experience and work samples alongside marks. This is a suggested way to organise follow-up, not a validated diagnostic checklist.

If progress remains limited, return to the original observations: was the support delivered, was the task appropriate, and is another need being missed? Assessment may clarify several contributing factors without producing one simple explanation. Revisit the plan with the relevant professionals. Improvement takes different forms and timeframes; neither a perfect home routine nor a specialist appointment guarantees top grades.

Escalate concerns that cannot wait for a school review

Seek prompt professional assessment when the decline is substantial or continuing, particularly with distress, changed sleep or appetite, withdrawal or difficulty attending school. Do not postpone help until the next report card or until a child has failed repeatedly. A learning concern and a mental-health concern can need attention at the same time.

If the child talks about hurting themselves or someone else, or behaves unsafely, seek immediate professional help. Use local emergency services for immediate danger or if you cannot keep someone safe. School targets and homework can wait while safety is addressed. A child asking for help should not have to prove that their grades are bad enough first.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use concrete observations and the child’s account to guide educational and health assessment.

Match support to identified needs, with appropriate language access and coordination.

Review learning and wellbeing, recognising that a single cause or guaranteed outcome may not be found.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise questions and observations for school and healthcare appointments. It cannot diagnose a learning or mental-health condition, interpret an intelligence score or determine educational entitlements.

When to seek help

Obtain prompt safeguarding help for suspected abuse or violence. Unsafe behaviour or talk of hurting oneself or others needs immediate professional help. Immediate danger or inability to keep someone safe requires local emergency services. Do not change prescribed medicine without the prescriber’s advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Describe what changed, when it began and which tasks are difficult.
  • Consider health, learning, language, emotional and access needs together.
  • Listen to the child and investigate safety concerns without blame.
  • Coordinate manageable support with school and the relevant professionals.
  • Review progress and seek immediate help when safety is at risk.

Frequently asked questions

How can I prevent my child from falling behind?

Support routines, accessible teaching and a workable place to study, and raise concerns early. Reducing distractions can help, but it cannot prevent every difficulty. Ask what is getting in the way of the specific task rather than expecting a perfect home environment to guarantee success.

Can arguments between parents affect schoolwork?

Family conflict can add stress and make concentration harder, but it does not explain every school problem. Reduce the child’s exposure to conflict and seek appropriate support. Avoid blaming either the child or one family event for all changes in learning.

What can cause a decline in school performance?

Possible contributors include health or sensory problems, missed teaching, learning or language needs, emotional distress and difficulties at home or school. Several can occur together. The pattern, the child’s account and a coordinated assessment help identify useful next steps.

Are phones and tablets responsible for falling grades?

Not automatically. Look at content, timing, interruptions and whether use displaces sleep or work. Digital tools can also support learning. Agree practical changes, then check what improves; do not assume a device ban settles the wider question.

Does poor school performance mean low intelligence or ADHD?

No. Grades alone cannot establish either, and a learning disability does not mean low intelligence. Ask for an assessment of the actual difficulty. Health, language, teaching opportunities and emotional wellbeing also affect what a child can show at school.

Who should I contact first?

Speak with the teacher or learning-support lead and the child’s usual healthcare professional. Bring examples, relevant health information and the child’s views. They can help select further assessment. Seek immediate professional help for unsafe behaviour or statements about harming anyone; immediate danger requires emergency services.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
